lead: A grammar says which strings are sentences; a parser proves that one particular string is a sentence and returns its trees. Trying rules blindly takes exponential time, so both standard algorithms use a table instead. CYK fills a triangular table of word spans, bottom-up, and needs the grammar in Chomsky normal form. Earley walks the sentence left to right carrying dotted rules and accepts any CFG. Both run in polynomial time.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for CFG rules and trees, and 3.2 for Chomsky normal form, which CYK requires.

sections.h3: Recognition, trees, and three families of parser

blocks.text: A context-free grammar is G = (N, Σ, P, S): N is the set of nonterminals such as NP, Σ is the set of terminal words, P is the set of rules, and S is the start symbol. Parsing answers two questions. Recognition asks whether a word string w = w₁w₂…wₙ is in L(G). Tree extraction asks for the parse trees themselves.

The number of possible trees grows fast: 14 binary trees over 5 leaves, 4862 over 10. Testing them one by one is exponential, so every practical algorithm stores the answer to each subproblem once. That store is a chart: a table indexed by positions in the sentence.

Top-down parsing starts at S and expands rules until the leaves match the words. Recursive descent writes one function per nonterminal and reads like the grammar. Its weakness is left recursion: a rule A → A α makes the function call itself on the same input forever. Rewriting the grammar to remove left recursion, or replacing recursion with an explicit stack and a loop, removes the loop.

Bottom-up parsing starts at the words and joins them into nonterminals. CYK is a bottom-up chart parser over spans; Earley is a left-to-right chart parser over dotted rules. Shift-reduce parsing, a bottom-up method that uses a stack, is in 3.8.

sections.h3: CYK: a triangular table of spans

blocks.text: The Cocke–Younger–Kasami algorithm assumes Chomsky normal form, so every rule is either A → B C or A → a. Conversion is in 3.2.

items: n is the number of words. Make one cell (i, j) for every pair with 1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ n: n(n+1)/2 cells, a triangle.
Cell (i, j) holds the set of nonterminals that derive words i to j, both ends included.
Length 1: put A in (i, i) if the rule A → wᵢ exists.
Lengths L = 2 to n: for (i, j) with j = i + L − 1, try every split k from i to j − 1. If B is in (i, k), C is in (k+1, j), and A → B C is a rule, add A to (i, j).
Accept when S is in (1, n).

blocks.where: n is the number of words; |G| is the number of grammar rules; splits(n) counts the (i, k, j) triples tried. For n = 5 that is 20.

blocks.text: Each nonterminal is stored once per cell, even when two splits both produce it. That discarding of multiplicity keeps the run polynomial instead of exponential.

Recognition is not a tree. To print one, store a back pointer whenever a nonterminal is added: the split k and the rule A → B C. Reading pointers back from (1, n) rebuilds the tree. For the best tree under a probability model see 3.5; the loop is the same with a maximum in place of set union.

sections.h3: Earley: dotted rules read left to right

blocks.text: An Earley state is a rule with a dot and an origin, written (A → α · β, i). The parser is working on A → αβ, has matched α, the dot sits before β, and i is the position where this rule started.
There is one chart set per position, S₀ to Sₙ; a state in S_j has its dot after j words. S₀ starts with (S′ → · S, 0), where S′ is a fresh start symbol.

items: PREDICTOR: a state (A → α · B β, i) in S_j predicts every rule of B: add (B → · γ, j) to S_j for each rule B → γ.
SCANNER: a state (A → α · a β, i) in S_j with a a word. If word j+1 is a, add (A → α a · β, i) to S_{j+1}.
COMPLETER: (B → γ ·, i) in S_j means B covers words i+1 to j. For each (A → α · B β, k) in S_i, add (A → α B · β, k) to S_j.
Accept when (S′ → S ·, 0) is in S_n.

blocks.text: Repeat the moves until no set grows; they are steps inside one pass, not three algorithms.
T(n) = O(n³) general,  O(n²) unambiguous grammar,  O(n) bounded-state grammar
blocks.where: n is the number of words. A bounded-state grammar is one where no chart set S_j ever holds more than a fixed number of states, however long the sentence is; most programming-language grammars are of this kind.

blocks.text: Earley accepts any CFG: left recursion, ε rules and unit rules need no rewriting. The price is bookkeeping: each set holds many states and each new state must be checked against those already present.

head: CYK
Earley
rows: possible in CNF; span order handles it, no rewriting needed

blocks.text: Use CYK when the grammar is already normalised, for a short program, or for the inside score of a probabilistic grammar. Use Earley when the grammar is written naturally: a hand-written English grammar, or a language grammar with long rules.

figure.caption: The highlighted cell (1,5) holds S, so the whole sentence is accepted. It is built at split k = 2 from NP in (1,2) and VP in (3,5).

spec.title: CYK table, 'the boy ate the cake'
spec.aria: A triangular CYK table for the five-word sentence, with NP in cell (1,2), VP in cell (3,5), and S in cell (1,5), so the sentence is accepted.

examples.question: Grammar in CNF: S → NP VP; NP → Det N; VP → V NP; Det → the; N → boy | cake; V → ate. Run CYK on 'the boy ate the cake' and say whether it is accepted. Count the split checks for n = 5.
steps: Words: w₁ = the, w₂ = boy, w₃ = ate, w₄ = the, w₅ = cake. n = 5, so the table has 5·6/2 = 15 cells.
Length 2: (1,2) uses split k = 1, Det in (1,1) and N in (2,2), so NP. (2,3) and (3,4) are empty. (4,5) gives NP from Det in (4,4) and N in (5,5).
Length 3: (1,3) and (2,4) empty. (3,5) uses split k = 3, V in (3,3) and NP in (4,5), so VP. Split k = 4 gives nothing because (3,4) is empty.
Length 4: (1,4) and (2,5) both need a cell that is empty, so both stay empty.
Length 5: (1,5) with split k = 2 gives NP in (1,2) and VP in (3,5), so S from S → NP VP. Splits k = 1, 3, 4 add nothing.
Split checks: length 2 uses 4; length 3 uses 6; length 4 uses 6; length 5 uses 4. Total 20, matching 5·4·6/6.
examples.answer: S is in cell (1,5), so the sentence is accepted, and the run makes 20 split checks.

traps: Running CYK on a grammar that is not in CNF. A rule A → B C D or a unit rule A → B fills cells wrongly; convert first.
Reading cell (i, j) as words i to j−1. It is i to j inclusive, so (1, n) is the whole sentence and a span of length 1 has i = j.
Stopping at the first split k that fills a cell. Every split must be tried; a later split may add a different nonterminal and change whether S reaches (1, n).
Saying CYK is O(n²) because the table has O(n²) cells. Filling one cell costs O(n) splits, so the total is O(n³ · |G|).

quiz.q: Which normal form does CYK require, and which rule shapes does it allow?
quiz.a: Chomsky normal form: A → B C with two nonterminals, or A → a with one terminal word, plus S → ε for the start symbol only, when the empty string must be generated.

quiz.q: What does the Earley state (VP → V · NP, 2) say?
quiz.a: Rule VP → V NP is being applied, V is already matched, the dot is before NP, and the rule started at position 2, i.e. after two words.

quiz.q: For n = 7 words, how many cells has the CYK table and how many split checks are made?
In the worked example, which cell holds NP for the words 'the boy', and from which two cells is it built?
quiz.a: Cell (1,2), built at split k = 1 from Det in (1,1) and N in (2,2) using NP → Det N.

quiz.q: Recursive descent loops forever on A → A α, but Earley does not. Why?
quiz.a: Recursive descent calls the A function again at the same input position, so no word is consumed. Earley's predictor adds (A → · A α, j) to S_j with the same j; the second time it is produced the state is already in the set and is dropped.

quiz.q: Earley is O(n³) in general but O(n²) for an unambiguous grammar. Why?
quiz.a: In an unambiguous grammar each span has essentially one analysis, so the number of completing states over a span stays bounded. The completer then does quadratic work instead of paying a third factor for many pairings of the same span.

quiz.q: CYK reports only that S is in (1,5). What extra information turns this into a parse tree?
quiz.a: Back pointers: for each nonterminal stored in a cell, record the split k and the rule A → B C that added it. Reading them back from (1, n) rebuilds the tree.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real parsers store all parses of a span in a packed parse forest, so an exponential number of trees fits in polynomial space; an Earley parser with a shared packed parse forest is the standard form. Leo's optimization makes right recursion linear in Earley, and the same span table with a maximum instead of a set gives the Viterbi CYK used inside statistical machine translation. Search next for 'Earley SPPF', 'Viterbi CYK' and 'packed parse forest'.
